title: 01 — Scale From Zero to Millions of Users
html:
01 — Scale From Zero to Millions of Users

The one idea: you scale a system by making the web tier stateless (so you can add boxes freely) and then by relieving the data tier — replicas for reads, caches for hot data, shards for everything else. Every step removes one bottleneck and introduces one new failure mode.

1. The journey, one step at a time

---
title: Scaling journey — one server to millions of users
---
flowchart LR
    S1["1 server<br/>web + DB"] --> S2["Split DB<br/>onto its own box"]
    S2 --> S3["Load balancer<br/>+ N web servers"]
    S3 --> S4["DB replication<br/>primary + read replicas"]
    S4 --> S5["Cache + CDN"]
    S5 --> S6["Stateless web tier<br/>session in shared store"]
    S6 --> S7["Multiple data centres"]
    S7 --> S8["Message queue<br/>async workers"]
    S8 --> S9["Sharding"]
Step Problem it solves New problem it creates
Separate DB server Web and DB fight for CPU/RAM Network hop between them
Load balancer + many web servers One web box is a SPOF and a ceiling Sessions stuck to one server
Primary/replica DB Reads swamp the primary; DB is a SPOF Replication lag → stale reads
Cache Repeated reads of hot data Invalidation, stampedes, cold starts
CDN Static assets travel across the world Cache busting on deploy
Stateless web tier Can't autoscale with sticky sessions Session store is now critical infra
Multi-DC Region outage; far-away users Data sync, geo-routing, split brain
Message queue Slow work blocks requests; spikes At-least-once delivery → idempotency
Sharding One DB can't hold the writes or data Cross-shard queries, resharding, hotspots

2. Vertical vs horizontal scaling

Vertical (scale up) Horizontal (scale out)
How Bigger box More boxes
Ceiling Hard limit (largest SKU) Practically none
Failover None — still one box Built in, if stateless
Complexity Trivial Needs LB, stateless design, distributed data
When Early; databases before sharding Web/API tiers from day one

⚠️ Scaling the database vertically first is usually correct. A large managed SQL instance goes a very long way, and sharding is a one-way door.

3. The web tier: make it stateless

A server is stateless when any instance can serve any request. Move out of process:

  • Session → distributed cache (Redis) or a signed token (JWT) the client carries.
  • Uploaded files → blob storage, never local disk.
  • In-memory caches that must be consistent → shared cache (local caches are fine for immutable data).
  • Scheduled jobs → a single scheduler or a leader-elected worker, not "every instance runs the cron".

Once stateless: put it behind a load balancer, autoscale on CPU / request rate, and deploy with rolling or blue-green releases.

4. The data tier

4.1 Replication

---
title: Primary–replica database replication
---
flowchart TB
    App["Web tier"] -->|writes| P[(Primary)]
    App -->|reads| R1[(Replica 1)]
    App -->|reads| R2[(Replica 2)]
    P -. async replication .-> R1
    P -. async replication .-> R2
  • Read-your-writes problem: a user saves, then reads from a replica that hasn't caught up. Fixes: read from the primary for a short window after a write, or pin the user's session to the primary for writes they just made.
  • Failover: a replica is promoted. Async replication means the last few writes may be lost — say so.

4.2 Cache

  • Cache-aside is the default: read cache → miss → read DB → populate cache with a TTL.
  • Cache things that are read often and change rarely. Set a TTL on everything.
  • Watch for stampede (many misses on one hot key at expiry) → request coalescing or early refresh with jitter.

4.3 Sharding

Split rows across databases by a shard key.

Pick a key that Because
Spreads writes evenly Otherwise one shard is the new bottleneck (celebrity problem)
Keeps a request on one shard Cross-shard joins/transactions are slow and complicated
Won't need to change Resharding is the most painful operation in the system

Use consistent hashing or a directory service so adding a shard doesn't move everything (→ chapter 05).

5. Multiple data centres

  • GeoDNS / Front Door routes users to the nearest healthy region.
  • Active-passive: simpler; the passive region is on standby; RPO > 0 with async replication.
  • Active-active: both serve traffic; needs conflict resolution or a clear per-entity home region.
  • Test failover regularly — an untested DR plan is a hypothesis.

6. Observability and automation — the steps nobody draws

At scale you need: logs (centralised, structured), metrics (host + business: DAU, orders/min), traces (cross-service latency), and CI/CD so a change can reach production many times a day safely. Without these, every step above makes the system harder to operate.

7. .NET / Azure mapping

Concept Azure / .NET
Load balancer (L7) Application Gateway, Front Door (global), or Azure Load Balancer (L4)
Stateless web tier App Service / Container Apps / AKS with autoscale rules
Session store Azure Cache for Redis + AddStackExchangeRedisCache / IDistributedCache
Read replicas Azure SQL geo-replicas or Hyperscale named replicas; ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly in the connection string
CDN Azure Front Door / Azure CDN in front of Blob Storage
Queue Azure Service Bus (commands), Event Hubs (event streams), Storage Queues (simple)
Sharding Azure SQL Elastic Database tools, Cosmos DB (partition key is the shard key)
Observability Application Insights + OpenTelemetry (AddOpenTelemetry().UseAzureMonitor())

8. Review checklist

  • Start with one box and grow — don't open with 40 microservices.
  • Name the bottleneck before adding the component that fixes it.
  • Mention replication lag and read-your-writes when you add replicas.
  • Mention invalidation and stampede when you add a cache.
  • Justify the shard key: even writes, single-shard requests, stable.
  • End with monitoring and what breaks next.
